newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, U.S. hold official meeting despite China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, U.S. hold official meeting despite China.

text.p: A senior U.S. official acknowledged holding an official meeting with Taiwan on trade issues Monday, despite the likelihood of an angry protest from Beijing.
"Our discussions were very valuable, very constructive," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told a news conference after concluding one day of economic talks with Taiwanese officials.
"These consultations will go forward in Washington in about one year," Summers said.

Beijing suggested last week that it would be unhappy about such meetings, reminding Washington that its establishment of diplomatic ties with China included a promise to have no official relations with Taiwan, including high-level visits.
Summers said such discussions with Taiwan would continue into the "indefinite future."
Summers is the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Taiwan since Transportation Secretary Federico Pena in was here December 1994.
His delegation met economics vice minister Hsu Ke-sheng and other financial and foreign affairs officials for wide-ranging talks that included bilateral and regional economic issues.
In a luncheon speech, Summers hailed the island's powerhouse economy and urged that it play a wider international role in Asia.
"I also look forward to the day when we can welcome Taiwan into the World Trade Organisation,," Summers told the American Chamber of Commerce.

Praising Taiwan's dramatic development in recent decades and its drive to liberalise its financial system, Summers called the island an "economic powerhouse" and -- alluding to its rivalry with China -- said Taiwan had a role to play in the WTO.

"I recognise there are political issues, but I nevertheless see it as a golden opportunity for Taiwan to increase its role in this important international organisation, and to play the part that it should as a major Asian economy," Summers said.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since they split in 1949 after a civil war, says the island is not entitled to membership as a sovereign nation in international bodies.
Beijing has said it would accept Taiwan's membership in the WTO as a customs territory, but not before China itself is allowed to join the world trade club.
The United States, Canada, Europe and Japan have cited China's market barriers in excluding it from the WTO.
The United States switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979 but keeps close, unofficial trade ties with Taiwan and has sought since 1994 to bolster economic relations.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but is not expected to gain entry before China is allowed to join.
